result: The MRSN sequenced 5,129 P. aeruginosa isolates from 71 facilities (2011-2020), identifying 547 STs. ST-621 represented 5% of isolates but 89% originated from a single facility (Facility A), showing high genetic relatedness (0-23 allelic differences by cgMLST). Patient transfers from Facility A were documented in three instances, while two other facilities had genetically distinct ST-621 strains.
evaluation: All reviewers affirm the genomic surveillance approach and data collection. The editor states the work presents 'convincing genomic analyses' and reviewers describe the genomic analyses as 'convincing' (Reviewer 2) with 'comprehensive descriptions' (Reviewer 1). No concerns were raised about the surveillance data or the identification of the ST-621 outbreak.

result: A total of 253 ST-621 isolates were collected from Facility A (a 425-bed level 1 trauma center) between May 2011 and December 2020, primarily from respiratory (42%) and urine (39%) samples. Phylogenetic analysis confirmed all isolates belonged to a single outbreak clone with an average distance of 38 SNPs (IQR 19). The outbreak involved 82 patients (average age 57.2±21.0, M/F ratio 1.7), with 56% contributing serial isolates and six patients showing prolonged carriage.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the phylogenetic characterization of the outbreak. Reviewer 2 notes 'convincing genomic analyses indicate spread throughout the hospital' and Reviewer 1 states the work 'comprehensively describe[s] the characteristics of a long-term Pseudomonas aeruginosa ST 621 outbreak.' The genetic relatedness data and patient demographics are not questioned.

result: Two outbreak subclones (SC1 and SC2) were identified with average distances of 24 and 31 SNPs respectively. ST-621 isolates were observed in 26 wards/units across all 7 floors of two buildings, but the subclones were spatially and temporally distinct. SC1 was predominantly in the Main Building (78%) and detected before 2014 (60%), while SC2 was mainly in the Tower Building (52%) and collected after 2014 (77%). SC1 spread early in Main Building ICUs (floors 2-3), while SC2 emerged in Tower Building ICUs (floor 3).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 3 states 'the authors were able to show that these two subclones emerged in two separate buildings of the hospital' as a strength. The editor highlights that analyses 'show how such data can help in...characterising the epidemic lineages.' The spatial-temporal distinction between subclones is accepted without challenge.

result: ER isolates were predominantly from urine cultures (92% vs 32% from other locations, p<0.0001) and 72% were serial isolates from returning patients. Between 2011-2016, an average of 11.5 new cases was detected annually, decreasing to 3 cases/year from 2017-2021. Overall P. aeruginosa cases at Facility A remained stable, though sampling was inconsistent due to staffing issues.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the temporal trends but note sampling limitations. Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'potential sampling bias due to partial sampling' as a limitation but states 'the work is still important.' Reviewer 2 notes 'sampling methodology was inconsistent' as a weakness but confirms in revision comments that 'all my concerns have been comprehensively addressed.' The decrease in cases is not disputed.

result: Genetic diversity in 2011 (16.3 SNPs average) suggested an earlier outbreak origin. Molecular clock analysis inferred the MRCA in 1999 (±3 years), shortly after the Main Building opened in 1996. SC1 and SC2 emerged concurrently with MRCAs dated to 2004 (±2 years), not as descendants but as concurrent lineages. SC2 was first sampled after the Tower Building opened in 2012, with the earliest isolate from patient 27 (wound infection). Fifteen serial isolates from this patient over 3 years were not monophyletic, with their MRCA coinciding with SC2 emergence.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the molecular clock dating. The editor states analyses 'show how such data can help in dating the origin of the outbreak' and Reviewer 2 notes 'convincing genomic analyses indicate spread throughout the hospital since the beginning of the century.' The concurrent emergence of subclones and dating to 1999 are accepted without challenge.

result: SNP distribution analysis showed a unimodal distribution (peak 40.5) for all isolates, but bimodal profiles (lower peaks at 12.4, 15.3, 11.6 SNPs) when selecting isolates from the same month, ward, or both. Only 10 patients met criteria for presumed patient-to-patient transmission (all SC1, mostly 2011-2012, six in ICU #1). Twelve cases met criteria for presumed environmental origin, including three patients in ICU #20 with SC2 isolates differing by only 0-4 SNPs despite years between collections. Environmental origin was predicted for seven of nine most recent patients (2018-2020), including five SC1 resurgence cases in ICUs #1-2.
evaluation: Reviewers express significant concerns about the transmission inference methodology. Reviewer 3 states as a 'major concern' that 'the authors used fixed thresholds and definitions to classify the origin of an infection' and 'were not able to give uncertainty measures around transmission routes.' Reviewer 2 notes 'epidemiological information was limited' and this 'complicat[es] inference of exact transmission routes.' While reviewers accept the data, they question the certainty of transmission route assignments.

result: Environmental sampling in 2021-2022 collected 159 swabs from 55 locations in 8 wards/units, confirming reservoirs of both SC1 and SC2 (n=17 isolates) in sink drains in seven patient rooms across wards #1, 2, 6, and 20 in both buildings. During this period, 56 additional clinical isolates (25 SC1, 31 SC2) from 13 patients (including 11 new cases) were collected, indicating ongoing transmission.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm the environmental sampling findings. Reviewer 3 states as a strength that 'the authors support their conclusions with prospective environmental sampling in 2021 and 2022 and link the role of persistent environmental contamination to sustaining nosocomial transmission.' The editor notes the work 'highlight[s] the value of routine surveillance of patients and environmental sampling.' Reviewer 1 emphasizes the work 'adds to the growing evidence implicating sinks as long-term reservoirs for important MDR pathogens.'

result: Outbreak isolates showed non-susceptibility to multiple antibiotic classes. Imipenem resistance increased from 63% (2011) to >95% (2014+), while cefepime resistance decreased from 81% to 37% (2011-2014). These temporal patterns were linked to SC1 decline and SC2 rise, with SC2 showing significantly higher imipenem resistance (98% vs 76%, p<0.001) and lower cefepime resistance (38% vs 66%, p<0.001) than SC1. Tobramycin and ciprofloxacin resistance remained stable.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the antibiotic resistance findings. Reviewer 2 notes 'ongoing transmission coincided with both increasing resistance without acquisition of carbapenemase genes' and Reviewer 1 states 'identifying the changes in resistance genes and virulence genes over time would not be possible without genomic data.' Reviewer 3 notes the study 'showed the emergence of antibiotic resistance to cephalosporin, carbapenems and colistin over time.' The statistical associations are not questioned.

result: Outbreak isolates contained no plasmids and carried only two acquired resistance genes (crpP, aac(6')-Ib4) besides intrinsic AmpC β-lactamase. From 164 resistance-associated genes, 68 distinct mutations (20 predicted LOF) were identified in 37 genes, with eight genes mutated independently ≥3 times. OprD was most frequently mutated (6 independent mutations, 5 LOF), including R318fs in 92 SC1 isolates and R6* in 115 SC2 isolates, both occurring early (2006-2008) but SC2-OprD-R6* only becoming predominant from 2014. AmpD W97* LOF (51 isolates) and PBP3 R504C (>50 isolates) were also prevalent. PBP3 R504C was acquired independently twice (SC1 in 2007, SC2 in 2014) and strongly associated with fourth-generation cephalosporin resistance.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the chromosomal mutation analysis. Reviewer 2 notes the work involves 'determining recurring mutations in outbreak isolates' as a strength. Reviewer 1 emphasizes 'identifying the changes in resistance genes and virulence genes over time would not be possible without genomic data.' The specific mutations and their temporal emergence are accepted without challenge.

result: NSY mutations in ColRS (3 sites, 4 isolates) and PmrAB (2 sites, 3 isolates) did not affect colistin MICs (4 mg/L, same as wild-type). However, Patient 2 (with colistin therapy history) acquired a PhoQ E77fs LOF mutation in two serial isolates, resulting in an 8-fold MIC increase (32 mg/L). This colistin-resistant strain emerged in early 2011 but remained constrained to a single patient with no further spread detected.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the colistin resistance findings. Reviewer 2 notes 'ongoing transmission coincided with...convergence of mutations towards a host-adapted lifestyle' and Reviewer 3 mentions 'the emergence of antibiotic resistance to...colistin over time.' The lack of spread of the colistin-resistant strain is not questioned, supporting the authors' conclusion about its limited transmission.

result: Genome-wide, 64 genes were mutated independently ≥2 times (excluding synonymous mutations), functionally enriched for signal transduction (28% vs 6% genome-wide, p<0.001) and cell wall/membrane biogenesis (17% vs 7%, p=0.0017). Six cell wall/membrane genes were recurrently mutated (including rmlA, betT2). Among signaling genes, various TCS involved in pathogenesis were represented (narXL, fleRS, cbrAB), with cbrAB being the most mutated locus (16 NSY mutations in 80 isolates). Sigma factor pvdS (6 NSY, 1 LOF), motility regulator morA (11 NSY, 2 LOF), and mucoidy system mucAB (4 sites, 3 LOF) were also recurrently mutated.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the genome-wide mutation analysis. Reviewer 2 states 'determining recurring mutations in outbreak isolates allows for insights into the evolution of potentially harmful pathogens' as a strength. Reviewer 1 notes 'identifying the changes in...virulence genes over time would not be possible without genomic data.' The functional enrichment findings are accepted without challenge.

result: NSY and LOF mutations were significantly enriched in genes for Type IV secretion system (0.59 sites/kb, p<0.001), flagellar biosynthesis/chemotaxis (0.21 sites/kb, p=0.0264), alginate production (0.31 sites/kb, p=0.0088), and O-antigen production (0.36 sites/kb, p=0.0126) compared to genome-wide distribution (0.11 sites/kb). WbpX D-rhamnosyltransferase (O-antigen pathway) was disrupted (S19fs) in 127 SC2 isolates, with PAUP predicting this occurred in 2005 (±24 months), concomitant with SC2 emergence.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the pathway enrichment analysis. Reviewer 2 notes the work shows 'convergence of mutations towards a host-adapted lifestyle' and Reviewer 1 emphasizes the value of 'identifying the changes in...virulence genes over time.' The statistical enrichment and temporal predictions are not questioned.

result: Five of six patients with long-term infections (>1 year) were SC2 carriers (9/11 for >6 months). All but one SC2 isolate carried truncated WbpX glycosyltransferase (essential for CPA biosynthesis). A convergence of mutations in genes for alginate production, quorum-sensing deficiency, loss of motility, and decreased protease secretion—all phenotypes associated with chronic infections—was observed throughout the 10-year sampling period.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the host adaptation findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'convergence of mutations towards a host-adapted lifestyle' as part of the outbreak characterization. Reviewer 1 states the work demonstrates 'long-term persistence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa ST 621 clones.' The association between SC2 and prolonged carriage is accepted without challenge.

result: The Main and Tower Buildings have distinct plumbing systems, providing ecological separation for subclone spread and divergence (aside from inter-hospital patient transfers). A recent study showed sinks in a newly built ICU were contaminated with P. aeruginosa outbreak clones before patient arrival.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the plumbing infrastructure as contributing to subclone separation. Reviewer 3 notes as a strength that 'detailed information on floor plans of the building and transfers between facilities was available' allowing the authors to show subclone emergence in separate buildings. The environmental contamination mechanism is affirmed by multiple reviewers emphasizing the sink reservoir findings.

result: Study limitations included: (1) partial and inconsistent sampling preventing capture of exact outbreak magnitude; (2) unavailable detailed epidemiological data (admission dates, bed locations, medications); (3) patient overlaps inferred only from location and culture dates, with many likely undetected; (4) fixed thresholds applied for transmission inference, leaving most case origins undetermined due to conservative criteria. TransPhylo is being explored as an alternative probabilistic approach.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these limitations. Reviewer 1 states 'potential sampling bias due to partial sampling' and 'lack of epidemiology data to support the interpretation' as weaknesses. Reviewer 2 notes 'epidemiological information was limited and the sampling methodology was inconsistent.' Reviewer 3 identifies as a 'major concern' that 'the authors used fixed thresholds' and 'were not able to give uncertainty measures.' All reviewers accept these as limitations but affirm the work remains valuable.

result: The study resulted in ongoing interventions at Facility A (closing sinks, replacing tubing, using foaming detergents). Near real-time sampling and sequencing of all P. aeruginosa isolates (not just MDR) commenced in 2021. As of May 2025, no new ST-621 cases have been reported in over 15 months, with only four cases identified in 2022-2024, confirming slowed spread.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the intervention impact. Reviewer 1 requested 'additional timeline indicating when routine surveillance was introduced and examples of actions or changes guided by the surveillance data that resulted in decrease in ST 621 transmission' to support the abstract's claim about successful infection control. The editor notes the work has 'direct infection control implications.' The decrease in cases following interventions is accepted as evidence of success.

result: The roll-out of routine WGS surveillance in clinics has the potential to improve patient care and prevent some of the estimated 136 million hospital-associated drug-resistant infections per year globally.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the broader implications for WGS surveillance. The editor states this is 'important work' that 'will be of interest to researchers concerned with the spread of drug-resistant bacteria in hospital settings.' Reviewer 1 notes the work 'could potentially motivate investments in generating and integrating genomic data into routine surveillance.' Reviewer 3 states 'the paper highlights the value of real-time surveillance and environmental sampling in slowing nosocomial transmission.'
